lead: An electronic control unit (ECU) is a small computer that runs the engine. Many times a second it reads its sensors, looks up calibrated tables called maps, and drives the injectors, the ignition coils and the valves. It exists because a three-way catalyst needs the air-fuel ratio held within about one percent of λ = 1 for the whole life of the car, through wear, heat and altitude, which no carburettor or mechanical distributor can do. Diesel engines also have an ECU, but they run lean (λ well above 1), meter the injected fuel directly and clean the exhaust without a three-way catalyst.
prereq: You need: the legal limits from emission norms, the air-fuel compromise from engine fuelling and exhaust emissions, and the targets in torque, power and BSFC.

sections.h3: Why a computer, and what a loop means

blocks.text: Here λ (the excess-air ratio) = actual air-fuel ratio ÷ stoichiometric air-fuel ratio; λ = 1.05 means 5 percent more air than the fuel needs. The three-way catalyst converts CO, HC and NOx at once only in a band about one percent wide around λ = 1. A carburettor meters fuel through fixed jets and a venturi; its mixture drifts with jet wear, fuel temperature, air density and altitude, and it cannot hold one percent over ten years and 150 000 km. The ECU can, because it measures and corrects.

Open loop means the ECU computes an output from its stored calibration alone. It looks up a number and fires the injector for that long, with no sensor confirming the result; it trusts that fuel pressure, airflow and injector flow are as calibrated.

Closed loop means a sensor measures the result and the ECU corrects the output. The exhaust gas oxygen (EGO, or lambda) sensor is the measuring element. A zirconia switching sensor gives about 0.1 V when the exhaust is lean and about 0.8 to 0.9 V when rich, and crosses over within a very small change of λ near 1; the ECU treats about 0.45 V as the switch point. It compares the reading with its target and adds a correction called a trim. An electronic table lookup alone is still open loop; only the measurement closes the loop.

The figure is the block diagram of an engine management system. Sensors on the left report speed, load, temperatures and exhaust oxygen. The ECU conditions and digitises them, runs the maps, and drives the actuators on the right. The exhaust gas reaching the oxygen sensor closes the fuel loop. Over the CAN bus the engine ECU shares data with the other ECUs of the car, such as the transmission, ABS and body controllers (see In-vehicle networks and CAN).

sections.h3: Inside the ECU: signals, maps and interpolation

blocks.text: Signal path. A sensor output is rarely ready for a processor. Signal conditioning scales it into the input range of the analogue-to-digital converter (ADC), filters noise and clamps voltage spikes. The ADC turns the voltage into a count: a 10-bit ADC with a 5 V reference gives 2¹⁰ = 1024 steps, so one count is 5 ÷ 1024 ≈ 4.9 mV. Pulse signals such as crank and camshaft position go to timer inputs that measure the time between teeth.

The processor runs its program from flash memory and keeps working values in RAM. Learned trims are kept in non-volatile memory (EEPROM or flash) in most modern ECUs; older ones kept them in keep-alive RAM, lost when the battery is disconnected. Driver stages are power switches, usually low-side MOSFETs that ground one end of an injector or coil, with a clamp that absorbs the inductive kick when the switch opens.

Calibration grid. The central object is a two-dimensional table, the map. One axis is engine speed in rpm; the other is load, either manifold absolute pressure (MAP) in kPa or air mass per stroke in mg. Each cell stores one calibrated value: injector open time, spark advance, target λ, EGR valve position or idle air position. The values come from engine mapping on a dynamometer and from road tests; filling them is called calibration.

blocks.where: y is the value wanted (for example injector open time in ms); x is the measured speed or load; (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) are the two neighbouring calibrated cells.

blocks.text: Between cells, the ECU interpolates linearly along each axis. When both speed and load fall between cells it uses the four surrounding cells: first along one axis, then along the other.

blocks.text: Air measurement. The ECU must know the air mass trapped each cycle to compute the fuel. Speed density computes it from manifold absolute pressure, intake air temperature, engine speed and a volumetric-efficiency map. Mass airflow measures it directly with a hot-film or hot-wire sensor in the intake. Both feed the same fuel calculation in electronic fuel control; the same speed and load index the spark map in spark timing control.

examples.question: In the injection-time map of a warm engine, the column for 2000 rpm holds 4.0 ms at 40 kPa manifold pressure and 6.0 ms at 50 kPa. The ECU reads 46 kPa. Find the injector pulse width, and the fraction of one four-stroke cycle it takes.
steps: 46 kPa lies between the calibrated cells at 40 kPa and 50 kPa in the 2000 rpm column, so interpolate along the load axis.
One revolution at 2000 rpm takes 60 ÷ 2000 = 0.030 s. A four-stroke cycle is two revolutions: 0.060 s = 60 ms.
Fraction of the cycle = 5.2 ÷ 60 = 0.0867, that is 8.7 %.
examples.answer: The injector is open for 5.2 ms, which is 8.7 % of the 60 ms four-stroke cycle.

traps: Calling a map-based output closed loop. A table lookup is open loop even though it is electronic; the loop closes only when a sensor measures the result.
Interpolating along the wrong axis. Use the two cells that bracket the measured load in the same speed column.
Mixing milliseconds and percent. Pulse width is a time in ms; duty is that time divided by the cycle time, and a four-stroke cycle is two revolutions.
Treating λ = 1 as the target everywhere. Full load runs rich in open loop, and cranking and warm-up ignore the cold λ sensor.
Thinking limp-home is normal running. It replaces a failed sensor with a substitute value and limits the engine; it keeps the car moving, not clean.

quiz.q: Define open-loop and closed-loop engine control in one sentence each.
quiz.a: Open loop computes the output from stored maps alone, with no measurement of the result. Closed loop measures the result with a sensor and corrects the output towards the target.

quiz.q: List the blocks from a sensor to an actuator in an engine management system.
quiz.a: Sensor → signal conditioning → ADC (or timer input) → processor with memory and maps → driver stage → actuator.

quiz.q: Why does a three-way catalyst force the ECU to hold λ within about one percent?
quiz.a: The catalyst converts CO, HC and NOx together only in a band about one percent wide around λ = 1. Rich of it CO and HC pass; lean of it NOx passes.

quiz.q: A warm-engine injection map at 3000 rpm stores 3.5 ms at 30 kPa and 5.5 ms at 40 kPa. The ECU reads 36 kPa. Find the pulse width and the percentage of one four-stroke cycle.
The lambda sensor wire breaks during a highway cruise. What does the ECU do?
quiz.a: It sees the signal stuck or out of range, stores a fault code and lights the warning lamp, drops the closed-loop trim and runs the base map (with its learned long-term trim) in open loop. The car keeps running with poorer emission control.

quiz.q: An injector is open for 6 ms in each four-stroke cycle at 2500 rpm. Find the cycle time and the duty.
Compare speed density and mass airflow as ways to know the air mass.
quiz.a: Speed density uses a MAP sensor, air temperature and a volumetric-efficiency map: cheap and robust, but it needs recalibration when cams or intake change. Mass airflow measures air directly and follows such changes, but the sensor costs more and can be fouled by dirt or oil.

quiz.q: What is deceleration fuel cut and why does it save fuel?
quiz.a: With the throttle closed above about 1500 rpm the ECU switches the injectors off; the wheels drive the engine, so no fuel is needed. Injection resumes near idle to avoid a stall.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production ECUs are calibrated with model-based methods and hardware-in-the-loop rigs, where an engine model runs in real time and the ECU drives it. A torque structure turns the driver's pedal into a torque request, then splits it into air, fuel and spark paths. Cylinder-pressure and ion-current sensing are studied for closed-loop combustion control. Search next for "model-based calibration", "hardware-in-the-loop" and "torque-based engine control".
